description: Hanging out with some Hooded Merganser ([145480840](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/145480840))

This was a surprise! I thought I was seeing Bufflehead hanging out near (but not quite with) some Hooded Merganser ([145480850](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/145480850)). Nut when I zoomed in... 😁
He didn't stay on the surface much, and I kept losing him. Finally I couldn't find him at all. But then I found her ([145480851](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/145480851))!
I'd been watching a male ([145480847](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/145480847)). I lost him, and found her!

These two landed near a group of Canada Geese, but took off following some Shoveler which flew by. The Shoveler seemed to be too fast, and the Bufflehead broke off their chase. The Shoveler ([145480855](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/145480855)) came back and landed, and the Bufflehead joined them.

Bufflehead (Bucephala albeola) is a small sea duck of the genus Bucephala, the Goldeneyes. Adult males are striking black and white, with iridescent green and purple heads and a large white patch behind the eye. Females are grey-toned with a smaller white patch behind the eye and a light underside. Buffleheads are migratory and most of them winter in protected coastal waters, or open inland waters, on the east and west coasts of North America and the southern United States.

These Goldeneye birds were  swimming upstream away from me, along with some Hooded mergansers. Since I took one initial photo of them I switch my attention to the mergansers. After taking a few photos of that species -I turned my attention back to these goldeneyes, but they were just about to get beyond some riparian trees at the curve of the river, which would of been been beyond what I could see. But low and behold, they stopped and turned. 

This is basically what these two photos captured -the point were they stopped and turned.

Set 2, post disturbance, is here:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/150278057

Not Going To Turn Around
While standing on the pier I spotted a male bufflehead way out on the bay.  It was finishing up a bath with a wing flap which is always fun to photograph.  I was hoping it would turn around so I could see the pretty colors on the front of the head.

You Can't Make Me

Buffleheads Are Back
Another winter duck I look forward to every year.  One of the hardest ducks to photograph.  All that white plus they don't come very close.  These two males were a long way out on the lake so a highly cropped shot.

Photo 2:
Disappearing Act
One of the challenges with buffleheads is the way they suddenly disappear.  One moment you have focus & are about to take the shot, the next all you see is a ripple in the water.  And no idea where they will pop back up.  They swim a good distance underwater before resurfacing.  This time I caught one in the act.

description: I was observing this pair of Buffleheads while they were diving for food just offshore from Alki Beach.  It was well below freezing but clear and calm. I was attempting to capture the moment of a dive, just before their bill enters the water.  I wasn't successful although I did manage to capture a couple of instances when they arched forward with only the tip of a bill submerged.  It happens in a fraction of a second.  All of a sudden, the female initiated a takeoff and the male followed suit.  I was able photograph a nice sequence as they splashed and flapped their way to my right and parallel to the shore.  They were perfectly synchronized as can be seen here.

description:
First two pics = best ones, then in reverse time order; I saw him from the west side, then while he was diving and twiddling around I was able to cross the bridge, catch up to him, and get ahead of him at the boathouse dock to try and get closer as he went by. He was in no big hurry. Last few pics are him making his weird little kazoo quack (did not get audio but sounded like the clip labeled “male calls” here: https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Common_Goldeneye/sounds) and then comparison shots as he went past a mallard, a merganser who started to assertively roll up on him then changed his mind, a merganser napping with head under wing which I thought was cute, and a goose.

Super difficult to get good photos, was still using the auto-focus at that time and the fact that he is *SO* high contrast black and white kept blowing out the photos, not helped by the fact that he was super glossy and shiny and when the sun hit at the right angle, his black head became super brilliant green.

This is the only golden-eye I’ve seen this year, a year or two ago there was a small flock of about a dozen on this same stretch of the river for a day or two in the winter, but I’m not sure if I ever got photos of them at that time.

description:
With Don Fraser; an eventually successful chase of the Purple Sandpiper. A few other birders were also looking for the sandpiper; at least one left before it was found. The weather at the start was clear and chilly with fairly strong north winds and a low tide, becoming sunny, warm, and breezy with a fairly high, still-incoming tide by the end. We walked from one jetty to the other numerous times, and to the boat ramp at the northern end of the peninsula twice. Eventually, Don stationed himself at the southern jetty while I stayed at the northern jetty, which proved to be the jetty popular with the birds. I stared at the same 22 Ruddy Turnstones dozens of times until 1229, when a flock of 33 turnstones arrived -- shorebirds and larids had been filtering in to the rocks on the north jetty for more than 90 minutes as the rising tide inundated all offshore oyster bars. Although none of us saw the Purple Sandpiper fly in, it must have arrived with the large turnstone flock, as Anne Ruben found it a minute later. I was between the Purple Sandpiper and the rest of the birds, so I waited until the sandpiper flew to join all the other birds before I moved. All in all, it was a fun trip -- except for the ubiquitous kids and others who habitually harassed the Black Skimmers and other birds that were trying to rest on the beach.

Some numbers:

Greater Scaup, 7 in one flock, mostly males; other flocks farther out were probably also Greater Scaup
Bufflehead 40
American Oystercatcher 30, including two color-marked
Spotted Sandpiper 3, all photographed
Ruddy Turnstone 55 (precise count)
Sanderling 24
Laughing Gull 350
Ring-billed Gull 125
American Herring Gull 5
Blac Skimmer 95, including one color-marked
Royal Tern 25
Horned Grebe 10
Common Loon 9
American White Pelican 25 (21, 1, and 3)
